n: God calls Abram to leave everything familiar—homeland, relatives, and father’s household—and go to a land God will reveal. Abram’s journey of faith begins with trusting God without knowing exactly where he is going.

f.w: Get thee out of thy country

n: God promises Abram a great nation, blessing, and a great name. Unlike the builders of Babel, who tried to make a name for themselves, Abram receives a name as God’s gift—and he is to be a blessing to others.

This is the heart of the Abrahamic covenant: through Abram all the world’s families will be blessed. The book of Abraham explains this includes the gospel, the priesthood, and eternal life for all who receive it.

f.w: in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed

n: Abram obeys and leaves Haran with his nephew Lot. Genesis gives his age as seventy-five; the book of Abraham says sixty-two, perhaps counting a different departure.

f.w: So Abram departed, as the LORD had spoken unto him

f.g: Abraham 2:14 says Abraham was sixty-two when he left Haran.

n: Abram brings his family, wealth, and “the souls that they had gotten in Haran.” The book of Abraham explains these were people they had converted to the Lord.

f.w: the souls that they had gotten in Haran

n: Abram reaches Shechem, at the great tree of Moreh in the heart of Canaan. The land is already occupied by Canaanites—the promise will take faith and time.

f.g: Shechem, a town in the central hill country between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim.
Better “the oak (or terebinth) of Moreh,” perhaps a well-known sacred tree. Moreh means “teacher.”

n: The Lord appears and promises this very land to Abram’s descendants. Abram responds by building an altar—worship marks his path through the land.

f.w: Unto thy seed will I give this land

n: Abram moves to the hills between Bethel and Ai, builds another altar, and calls on the Lord’s name. His life becomes a trail of altars and prayers.

f.g: Means “house of God”; it receives this name later from Jacob (28:19).
Ai, a town east of Bethel (Joshua 7:2).

f.w: called upon the name of the LORD

n: Abram keeps moving south toward the Negev, the dry region of southern Canaan.

f.g: Toward the Negev, the arid southern land.

n: A severe famine strikes, and Abram goes down to Egypt, whose Nile River made its crops more reliable. Famine drives several patriarchs to Egypt, a pattern that will shape Israel’s story.

f.g: To live somewhere temporarily as a foreigner.

n: Abram realizes that Sarai’s beauty could endanger them. Though she was about sixty-five, people then lived longer, and she was still striking.

f.w: a fair woman to look upon

n: Abram fears that the Egyptians will kill him to take Sarai.

f.g: In the ancient world, a powerful ruler might eliminate a husband to claim his wife.

n: Abram asks Sarai to say she is his sister. The book of Abraham records that the Lord instructed Abraham to do this. Sarai was in fact his half-sister (20:12).
As expected, the Egyptians notice Sarai’s beauty.
Pharaoh’s officials praise Sarai to the king, and she is taken into his household, presumably to become a wife.

f.g: The title of Egypt’s king, meaning “great house.”

n: Pharaoh treats Abram well and gives him livestock and servants. The gifts suggest Pharaoh considered them a bride-price.
The Lord protects Sarai by striking Pharaoh’s household with plagues. God guards the mother of the promised line—foreshadowing the later plagues on Egypt in Moses’ day.
Pharaoh confronts Abram, sensing that the plagues came because Sarai was married.

f.w: What is this that thou hast done unto me?
f.g: The same kind of question God asked Eve (3:13).

n: Pharaoh returns Sarai and tells them to leave. The foreign king behaves honorably once he knows the truth.

f.w: take her, and go thy way

n: Pharaoh sends Abram away with all he had. Like Israel later, Abram leaves Egypt richer than he arrived.
